chapter: Behaviour of Gases and the Mole Concept
trick: A mole is just a counting word, like a dozen, only very much bigger: 6.022 × 10²³ of anything. One mole of a substance weighs its molecular mass in grams and, if it is a gas at STP, occupies 22.4 litres. Those three facts answer nearly every mole question.

video.query: mole concept Avogadro number molar volume numericals class 10 chemistry

data.prompt: Work this mole calculation through, one step at a time.
data.problem: How many moles are there in 88 g of carbon dioxide, and how many molecules is that? (C = 12, O = 16)

steps.ask: First, what is the molecular mass of CO2?
steps.why: Carbon 12 plus two oxygens at 16 each, that is 12 + 32 = 44.

steps.ask: So how many moles are there in 88 g?
steps.why: Moles equal mass divided by molar mass, so 88 ÷ 44 = 2. Dividing the wrong way round is the usual slip here.
Multiply the moles by Avogadro's number: 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules.

steps.ask: What volume would this occupy at STP?
steps.why: One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 litres at STP, so two moles occupy 44.8 litres. Note this holds for any gas, whatever its molecular mass.

data.answer: 2 moles, which is 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules and 44.8 litres at STP.

trick: Almost everything expands on heating, and water between 0 and 4 degrees is the famous exception that contracts instead. That single anomaly is why ice floats and why fish survive a frozen pond, and it is asked about far more often than ordinary expansion.

video.query: thermal expansion anomalous expansion of water conductivity class 10 physics

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about heat.

items.statement: Water contracts when heated from 0 to 4 degrees Celsius.
items.why: This is the anomalous expansion of water. It is densest at 4 degrees, which is why ice floats and why a pond freezes from the top down.

items.statement: Metals are generally better conductors of heat than non-metals.
items.why: Free electrons carry the energy through the metal, which is why a metal spoon in hot tea heats along its length and a wooden one does not.

items.statement: A gap is left between rails so that the train runs more quietly.
items.why: The gap allows for expansion in summer heat. Without it the rails would buckle.

items.statement: Heat always flows from a body of higher temperature to one of lower temperature.
items.why: Temperature, not the amount of heat contained, decides the direction of flow. A large cold object still gives heat to nothing hotter than itself.

items.statement: Air is a good conductor of heat.
items.why: Air is a poor conductor, which is exactly why woollen clothes, which trap air, keep us warm.

trick: Metal plus non-metal usually means electrons are transferred, so the bond is ionic; non-metal plus non-metal means they are shared, so it is covalent. Ionic compounds then dissolve in water and conduct when molten, and covalent ones generally do neither.

video.query: ionic and covalent bonding properties solubility class 10 chemistry

data.prompt: One of these compounds is not ionic. Which, and why?
data.because: The other four are each a metal joined to a non-metal, so electrons are transferred and the bond is ionic. Methane is carbon and hydrogen, two non-metals, so the electrons are shared and the bond is covalent — which is why methane is a gas at room temperature while the other four are hard, high-melting solids.

trick: Every extraction runs the same way: get rid of the rock, turn the ore into an oxide, take the oxygen off, then clean up. Concentration, roasting or calcination, reduction, refining. Once you know the sequence you can place any named process in it.

video.query: metallurgy extraction of metals roasting calcination reduction class 10 chemistry

data.prompt: Put the stages of extracting a metal from its ore into order.

items.label: Crushing and grinding the ore
items.note: Breaking the lumps down so the later steps can work

items.label: Concentration of the ore
items.note: Removing the gangue, by froth flotation or magnetic separation

items.label: Roasting or calcination
items.note: Heating to convert the ore into the oxide; roasting in air for sulphides, calcination without air for carbonates

items.label: Reduction of the oxide to the metal
items.note: With carbon, or by electrolysis for the very reactive metals

items.label: Refining the crude metal
items.note: Usually electrolytic refining, to get the pure metal
